front_page.title: MYC targeted de novo binders impair tumor growth
front_page.subject: biochemistry
front_page.reason: de novo binders against disordered MYC regions shrink tumors in vivo
front_page.abstract: MYC is one of the most frequently dysregulated oncogenic drivers across many cancers, yet direct therapeutic targeting has remained difficult because its function is mediated by disordered regions and transient protein-protein interactions. Here we design proteins that bind epitopes within regions of MYC whose sequence is conserved between human and mouse, including intrinsically disordered motifs required for oncogenic activity. In vitro, the designs bind MYC with nanomolar affinity and in cells they engage MYC, disrupt interactions with MAX, and remodel MYC-associated protein complexes. Expression of the binders decreases cell proliferation across diverse MYC-dependent hematopoietic, liver, pancreatic, and patient-derived tumor models, and in an orthotopic pancreatic cancer model, binder-expressing tumor cells were selectively depleted. This work establishes de novo protein design as a generalizable strategy to therapeutically target intrinsically disordered transcription factors.
front_page.why: Designed binders target conserved intrinsically disordered epitopes on MYC itself, depleting MYC-dependent tumor cells across five cancer models where small molecules have never worked.

front_page.title: Complex enzyme active site scaffolding by iteratively detuned catalytic guidance
front_page.subject: bioengineering
front_page.reason: classifier-free guidance fading on RF3 for multi-constraint catalytic sites
front_page.abstract: De novo enzyme design requires sequences whose structures reproduce prescribed catalytic geometries. This remains challenging for active sites that couple multiple catalytic residues, cofactors and substrates. Here we introduce the Catalytic Guidance Engine (CaGE), which optimizes designed sequences to satisfy complex sets of functional constraints by alternating constraint guided structure prediction trajectories with sequence design, gradually fading the strength of the constraint information over cycles to nudge the designed sequence towards satisfying all the constraints. We train RF3 to accept atom-pair distances and other design conditions, and use classifier-free guidance to fade their influence over multiple design cycles. We also develop training-free motif guidance protocols which operate at inference time by directly adjusting selected atoms towards the design target geometry during diffusion sampling. CaGE improves catalytic-motif geometry across a diverse enzyme benchmark and yields sequences that recover complex target active sites in independent AF3 predictions. We experimentally demonstrate the power of CaGE by designing active enzymes with complex catalytic sites: a nonheme-iron design positions four active-site residues around an iron centre and a transition-state ligand, and a PLP-dependent design positions four catalytic residues around a PLP cofactor with multiple functional groups. Active site substitutions and a 2.7[A] crystal structure support the designed mechanisms and structures. Thus, CaGE provides a route to functional de novo enzymes with complex active sites.
front_page.why: Fades classifier-free guidance on RF3 over repeated design cycles so a sequence settles into satisfying several catalytic-geometry constraints at once, instead of fighting them simultaneously.

front_page.title: Generative steering to adapt proteins beyond native biological contexts
front_page.subject: bioengineering
front_page.reason: test-time annealing sampler deimmunizes and recontextualizes proteins beyond native use
front_page.abstract: Proteins evolved for native biological contexts often fail when deployed in new cellular environments or therapeutic settings. We present ProVADA, a test-time framework that steers a pretrained protein generator toward externally defined properties while preserving functional constraints. Its Mixture-Adaptation Directed Annealing sampler combines coordinated mutations, population selection, and annealing to navigate rugged objective landscapes. Experimentally, ProVADA converted secreted human renin into an active, drug-inhibitable cytosolic protease and extensively deimmunized two murine single-chain antibody fragments to reduce HLA visibility while retaining antigen recognition. ESCAPE-seq measurements confirmed substantial depletion of HLA-I binder peptides across alleles. Deimmunized FMC63 variants retained CAR-T-cell killing and showed fewer binders than a tested humanized comparator. Together, these results demonstrate that broad sequence redesign can adapt functional proteins to non-native biological contexts.
front_page.why: A test-time annealing sampler converts secreted human renin into an active cytosolic protease and strips HLA-binder epitopes from antibody fragments, without retraining the generator.

front_page.title: Structural analysis of de novo-designed binders targeting the closed state of HSP90.
front_page.subject: Structure (London, England : 1993)
front_page.reason: cryo-EM confirms BindCraft-designed binders selectively lock closed-state HSP90
front_page.abstract: Heat shock protein 90 (HSP90) assists the folding and maturation of numerous signaling proteins and is an important therapeutic target. Most HSP90 inhibitors target the ATP-binding pocket and disrupt ATP-induced closure, whereas inhibitors targeting the closed state have not been developed. Here, we report de novo-designed protein binders that selectively recognize closed HSP90. Two binders, H2 and H4, have similar folds and affinities for HSP90 but distinct binding kinetics. Cryo-EM structures of HSP90 complexes with H2 and H4 revealed high accuracy of the BindCraft predictions. H2 and H4 compete with p23 at one, but not both, symmetrical p23-binding sites. In HEK293T cells, H2 induced a reduced heat shock response compared with the ATP-site inhibitor 17-DMAG while reducing levels of CDK4, providing functional evidence for HSP90 inhibition. These binders provide tools for probing HSP90 function and potential leads for developing closed-state HSP90 inhibitors.
front_page.why: Cryo-EM confirms BindCraft's predicted structures atom-for-atom, and the two designed binders selectively lock HSP90's closed conformation, a state no small-molecule inhibitor has ever reached.

front_page.title: Rigidity-Aware Geometric Pretraining for Protein Design and Conformational Ensembles
front_page.subject: bioinformatics
front_page.reason: geometric pretraining on 432K AF-DB structures before generative finetuning
front_page.abstract: Generative models have recently advanced de novo protein design by learning the statistical regularities of natural structures. However, current approaches face three key limitations: (1) Existing methods cannot jointly learn protein geometry and design tasks, where pretraining can be a solution; (2) Current pretraining methods mostly rely on local, non-rigid atomic representations for property prediction downstream tasks, limiting global geometric understanding for protein generation tasks; and (3) Existing approaches have yet to effectively model the rich dynamic and conformational information of protein structures. To overcome these issues, we introduce RigidSSL (Rigidity-Aware Self-Supervised Learning}, a geometric pretraining framework that front-loads geometry learning prior to generative finetuning. Phase I (RigidSSL-Perturb) learns geometric priors from 432K structures from the AlphaFold Protein Structure Database with simulated perturbations. Phase II (RigidSSL-MD) refines these representations on 1.3K molecular dynamics trajectories to capture physically realistic transitions. Underpinning both phases is a bi-directional, rigidity-aware flow matching objective that jointly optimizes translational and rotational dynamics to maximize mutual information between conformations. Empirically, RigidSSL variants improve designability by up to 43% while enhancing novelty and diversity in unconditional generation. Furthermore, RigidSSL-Perturb improves the success rate by 5.8% in zero-shot motif scaffolding and RigidSSL-MD captures more biophysically realistic conformational ensembles in G protein-coupled receptor modeling. The code is available at: https://github.com/ZhanghanNi/RigidSSL.git.
front_page.why: Pretrains on 432K AlphaFold-DB structures under simulated rigid-body perturbations before generative finetuning, front-loading geometric understanding instead of learning it incidentally from design labels.

front_page.title: De novo design of metalloenzymes using Metal Mer
front_page.subject: synthetic biology
front_page.reason: Metal Mer maps backbone geometry to metal sites, >99% ee
front_page.abstract: De novo enzyme design provides a route to create biocatalysts for target reactions, yet achieving high activity and selectivity directly from computation remains challenging. How best to design catalytic sites remains an open question, and enzyme design-metalloenzyme design for new-to-nature transformations in particular-is still limited in success rate, in substrate scope, and in the range of reactions accessible. Here we present a pipeline that produces efficient metalloenzymes directly from computation. It uses Metal Mer, a structural unit mapping backbone geometry to statistically preferred metal coordination modes, to build metal-binding sites with high confidence, and then constructs the catalytic core around the reaction product with geometric restrictions. Using the pipeline, we designed zinc-dependent hydride-transfer enzymes, obtaining a highly selective variant that exhibits enantiomeric excess (ee) >99% on 13 substrates without directed evolution. For steroid substrates bearing multiple carbonyl groups, redesigned variants achieved high regio- and diastereo- selectivity greater than 19:1. Applying this framework to iron-catalyzed alkene difunctionalization, designed variants were active out of the box (10% yield, 70:30 enantiomeric ratio (e.r.)), exceeding a previously reported natural functional analogs (<5% yield, <60:40 e.r.); a single active-site residue mutation further raised selectivity to 96:4 e.r. for several substrates, on par with extensively evolved natural enzymes. The crystal structure of an active design matches the computational model with a backbone RMSD of 0.4 Angstrom, supporting the accuracy of the approach. These results establish our design framework as a general strategy for the de novo design of metalloenzyme series with diverse coordination geometries and coordinating residues, enabling efficient and selective catalysis of challenging chemical transformations.
front_page.why: Metal Mer maps backbone geometry directly onto statistically preferred metal-coordination modes, then builds the catalytic core around the product, reaching >99% ee on 13 substrates with no directed evolution.

front_page.title: Seq2Pocket: Augmenting protein language models for spatially consistent binding site prediction.
front_page.subject: Bioinformatics (Oxford, England)
front_page.reason: structure-aware post-processing fixes fragmented pLM binding-pocket predictions
front_page.abstract: Protein-ligand binding site prediction (LBS) is important for many areas of structural biology and molecular modeling, where, as in other tasks, protein language models (pLMs) have shown great promise. In their application to LBS, the pLM classifies each amino acid as binding or not, but translating these predictions into three-dimensional binding pockets remains challenging; in particular, residue-centric predictions tend to produce spatially fragmented pockets. We present Seq2Pocket, a methodology for pocket-level LBS prediction that combines pLM finetuning, data enhancement, and structure-aware post-processing. First, we introduce sc-PDBenhanced, an extended training dataset that augments an existing sc-PDB dataset with additional small-molecule and ion-binding sites, improving coverage of non-obvious and small pockets. Second, we employ an embedding-supported smoothing classifier to refine residue-level predictions. Third, we define the Pocket Fragmentation Index and use it to select a clustering approach that preserves a consistent mapping between predictions and ground-truth pockets. We evaluate Seq2Pocket on two tasks: general binding site prediction using the LIGYSIS benchmark and cryptic binding site prediction using CryptoBench benchmark. Across both benchmarks, Seq2Pocket achieves state-of-the-art DCCtop-N and DCCtop-(N+2) performance. In particular, for general binding site prediction on the LIGYSIS benchmark, it improves distance-center-to-center recall by up to 13%, outperforming existing predictors. This improvement originates from training data quality rather than model architecture, as demonstrated by an ablation study. We believe that these findings contribute to more reliable evaluation practices in ligand binding site prediction, highlight the importance of training data curation, and provide pocket-level prediction tools that are better suited for downstream applications such as drug discovery. The Seq2Pocket web interface is available at https://seq2pocket.projekty.ms.mff.cuni.cz, running the ESM-2 650M variant. The sc-PDBenhanced is published using Zenodo platform at https://zenodo.org/records/18271517 [Škrhák and Hoksza 2026]. The models are published at HuggingFace: https://huggingface.co/skrhakv/seq2pocket. Supplementary data are available at Bioinformatics online.
front_page.why: Smooths residue-level pLM binding-site predictions with embedding-aware post-processing so the output pocket is one contiguous patch instead of scattered false fragments.

front_page.title: GOLD: Geometric Optimized Latent Diffusion for Structure-Aware RNA Inverse Folding
front_page.subject: cs.AI
front_page.reason: unified latent manifold co-diffuses RNA sequence and side-chain geometry
front_page.abstract: Designing RNA sequences that fold into specific 3D structures is a fundamental challenge in therapeutics. Current RNA inverse folding methods typically condition on 3D backbone coordinates but the generation is limited to 1D discrete sequences. This ignores the continuous side-chain orientations, which are essential for overall structural stability. To address this issue, we explicitly introduce side-chain geometry into the RNA generative process. Unlike co-design frameworks that diffuse across separate raw spaces, we propose Geometric Optimized Latent Diffusion (\textbf{GOLD}), which project sequence and structure into a unified latent manifold. GOLD employs a novel GeoVAE to elegantly integrate discrete RNA sequences with continuous side-chain angles. By mapping these modalities into a single, smooth latent manifold, GOLD naturally facilitates a synergistic co-diffusion process. To enhance structural validity, we further introduce a training-free, gradient-guided sampling mechanism. By decoding the generated sequence probabilities and side-chain geometries into structures during the sampling process, we compute analytical gradients from physical constraints. This dynamic feedback actively guides the generated sequence to a physically stable state. Extensive experiments validate the superiority of GOLD, achieving state-of-the-art performance across sequence recovery, secondary structure validity, and 3D foldability metrics. Our code and data are publicly available at https://github.com/darkflash03/GOLD.
front_page.why: Projects discrete RNA sequence and continuous side-chain angles into one shared latent manifold, so backbone and sequence co-diffuse instead of being generated in separate, incompatible spaces.

front_page.title: Relation-Aware Graph-Hypergraph Networks for Antibody Sequence-Structure Co-Design
front_page.subject: bioinformatics
front_page.reason: hypergraph encoder captures multi-body antibody CDR cooperative effects
front_page.abstract: Motivation: The design of antibody complementarity-determining regions (CDRs) is pivotal for therapeutic development, yet remains challenged by the complexity of the antibody-antigen interface. Existing methods, which largely rely on pairwise relationships, struggle to capture intrinsic multi-body interactions and global structural constraints. Results: We propose the Relation-Aware Graph-Hypergraph Network (RA-GHN), a framework that unifies graph-based pairwise modeling with biophysical hypergraphs to capture high-order cooperative effects. Its heterogeneous hypergraph uses epitope-paratope interaction patches, spatial structural clusters, and high-degree hub structures. A dual-pathway architecture integrates a Relation-Aware Equivariant Graph Network with an Equivariant Hypergraph Encoder while preserving SE(3)-equivariance. We also introduce the Structure-Sequence Decoupling Index, which balances structural reliability with sequence novelty. Experiments show that RA-GHN outperforms state-of-the-art baselines across standard benchmarks and affinity optimization tasks.
front_page.why: Models the antibody-antigen interface as a hypergraph instead of pairwise edges, so cooperative multi-residue effects in CDR design finally have an architecture built for them.

front_page.title: LigRNA: High-accuracy prediction of RNA-ligand binding sites via dynamic chemical complementarity and language model encoding
front_page.subject: bioinformatics
front_page.reason: GNN with cross-attention predicts RNA-ligand binding sites from structure and chemistry
front_page.abstract: RNA-binding small molecules represent a validated therapeutic modality, yet pinpointing their exact RNA binding sites remains critical for mechanistic understanding and drug optimization. Experimental methods, while precise, are costly and low-throughput, necessitating robust computational alternatives. Approaches based on static feature concatenation may overlook input-dependent relationships between RNA residues and ligand functional groups. Here we present LigRNA, a graph neural network framework that predicts RNA-ligand binding sites through joint cross-modal encoding of both molecules. LigRNA integrates structure-guided language model embeddings with physicochemical features-solvent-accessible surface area and secondary structure types, to construct comprehensive RNA representations. Ligands are encoded as attributed molecular graphs via graph attention networks, preserving atom-level chemical topology rather than compressing molecules into fixed fingerprints. A cross-attention mechanism then enables dynamic, ligand-dependent modulation of RNA nucleotide attention, capturing context-specific interaction patterns. Benchmarked on TE9 and TE18 datasets, LigRNA achieves F1 scores of 0.73 and 0.58, improving on GATRsite by 7.4% and 18.4%, respectively. Ablation studies identify the RNA residual encoder as the most consistent contributor across the two benchmarks. The source code is freely available at https://github.com/WillowWang0216/LigRNA.
front_page.why: Encodes ligands as attributed molecular graphs rather than fixed fingerprints, then cross-attends them against structure-aware RNA embeddings to predict exact binding residues instead of just binding or not.

blindspot.title: Kinetic-driven microphase separation and vitrification of crowded hydrogels with associative bonds.
blindspot.subject: Science advances
blindspot.abstract: The thermal response of stimuli-responsive hydrogels is typically viewed through thermodynamic equilibrium. However, in "crowded" networks with dense associative bonds, elasticity and diffusion kinetics dictate distinct nonequilibrium fates. We investigate thermal transitions of a PAAc-CaAc2 (polyacrylic acid complexed with calcium ions) hydrogel along two trajectories: a quasi-static isobaric pathway (path A) and a rapid quasi-isochoric pathway (path B). Along path A, the gel contracts homogeneously until reaching a hardening temperature via global vitrification (Thard). In contrast, path B triggers confined microphase separation into polymer-dense and dilute phases at a critical temperature (Tdem), followed by a hardening transition via localized vitrification ([Formula: see text]). We demonstrate that Tdem is governed by a mechanical-thermodynamic competition: The internal pressure (Pc) to trigger demixing scales linearly with the permanent-network shear modulus (Gx), maintaining a ratio of Pc/Gx ≈ 100. We identify Thard and [Formula: see text] as distinct hardening points, with elastically constrained local water content governing [Formula: see text]. This framework provides a strategy for programming nonequilibrium fates and "lockable" properties of responsive soft matter.
blindspot.why: A crowded associative-bond hydrogel resolves into either homogeneous vitrification or confined microphase separation depending purely on the competing timescales of elastic relaxation versus diffusive demixing along the approach trajectory, not on which state is the free-energy minimum.
blindspot.connection: This is a concrete kinetic-trap mechanism for the assembly-oracle problem: a subunit thermodynamically capable of closing into a shell can still arrest into an off-pathway aggregate if local bond-formation outruns global diffusive reorganization. An oracle trained only on structural or thermodynamic features of the target state, with no path-rate term, would systematically miss exactly this failure mode.

ml-method.title: DiffusionRVGE: Reinforcement Learning via Regression-Based Value Gradient Estimation
ml-method.subject: cs.AI
ml-method.reason: regression-based value-gradient estimation fine-tunes diffusion models with rewards, no backprop
ml-method.abstract: Reinforcement learning improves diffusion models using rewards on generated images, but repeated denoising and gradient estimation make training expensive. We introduce \method, an efficient method that constructs useful update directions by regressing centered rewards on centered final denoised images. It requires neither reward derivatives nor adjoint backpropagation through the sampling trajectory. A unified first-variation formulation identifies the value-gradient target with or without a trajectory-KL penalty. A population analysis under Gaussian noising explains the regression geometry, while a subspace analysis motivates clean-image coordinates. The implementation adapts rollout bandwidth and query weights to reward continuity: local rollouts suit smooth rewards, whereas broader groups provide informative contrasts for discrete rewards. Trained jointly on five rewards, one SD3.5-Medium model matches or exceeds DiffusionNFT's joint model on seven of eight metrics, reaching GenEval $0.94$, OCR $0.92$, and PickScore $23.82$ at about one fifth of its estimated training compute. In single-reward training, \method reaches matched reward thresholds $2.1$--$6.7\times$ faster than reproduced DiffusionNFT on identical hardware. Ablations support the clean-image estimator, direct direction transfer, and reward-dependent rollout choices. Code is available at https://github.com/jy-wang-tsinghua/DIFFUSIONRVGE.

ml-method.title: Blitz: Accelerating the Diffusion Modules of AlphaFold3 and Boltz-2
ml-method.authors_short: Vinay Saji Mathew, …, William K. M. Lai
ml-method.subject: cs.LG
ml-method.reason: consistency distillation cuts AF3/Boltz-2 diffusion from 200 to 8 steps
ml-method.abstract: Diffusion-based protein structure prediction models produce all-atom structures in about 200 denoising steps, and that cost has driven a number of few-step samplers. We present Blitz, a few-step distillation framework that uses a geometric noise schedule to distribute steps more evenly across noise scales, then learns those updates through multistep consistency training. Physical steering and target-free candidate selection help reduce the remaining geometric defects at inference. We apply Blitz to AlphaFold 3 and Boltz-2, reducing denoising from 200 steps to eight. Because published few-step results use different benchmarks and scoring procedures, we compare both distilled models with their teachers and other few-step methods under a common evaluation protocol covering structural accuracy, interface quality, ligand placement, and stereochemical validity. Blitz retains teacher-level structural accuracy, with AF3-Blitz outperforming all evaluated few-step baselines and exceeding its teacher on several accuracy metrics.

ml-method.title: ADT: All-Atom Diffusion Tokenizer for 3D Molecular Structures
ml-method.subject: cs.LG
ml-method.reason: diffusion tokenizer decouples token granularity from all-atom reconstruction resolution
ml-method.abstract: Discrete structural tokenization provides a promising route to autoregressive 3D molecular generation. Yet, existing tokenizers face a trade-off between compact representation and all-atom reconstruction: atom-level tokens preserve atomic details but produce long sequences, while compact residue-level protein tokens typically omit side-chain geometry. To overcome this limitation, we propose All-atom Diffusion Tokenizer (ADT), which decouples token granularity from reconstruction resolution. ADT uses one structural token per atom for small molecules and one token per protein residue that jointly represents backbone and side-chain geometry. To mitigate geometric distortion introduced by quantization, we leverage the generative capacity of diffusion models to recover fine-grained atomic geometry beyond deterministic decoding from discrete tokens. Extensive experiments across small molecules and proteins demonstrate that ADT achieves strong reconstruction from compact discrete representations while enabling high-quality autoregressive generation of both small molecules and all-atom protein structures. These results establish compact structural tokens as an effective discrete interface for all-atom molecular reconstruction and generation.

ml-method.title: Learning to Be Guided: Shaping Latent Geometry for Classifier-Free Guidance
ml-method.subject: cs.LG
ml-method.reason: prototype regularization shapes latent class geometry for better CFG
ml-method.abstract: Classifier-free guidance (CFG) is a standard component of conditional diffusion models, and guided generation performance has become the \textit{de facto} measure of state-of-the-art models. Recent work on latent diffusion models seeks to learn latent spaces that are easier to model with diffusion. However, under CFG, generation additionally depends on how conditions are arranged in the latent space. We study this arrangement under discrete class conditions, termed \emph{class geometry}, and investigate what class geometry allows a latent space to work well with CFG. Under a Gaussian class model, we show that shifting variance from intra- to inter-class at fixed total variance makes classes more distinguishable under noise, and derive a noisy posterior objective whose per-sample descent direction is proportional to the oracle CFG correction. Based on the analysis, we propose Prototype Regularization (PR), a lightweight surrogate for the intractable noisy posterior objective, which applies a cosine prototype classifier to spatially pooled latents. With a controlled training budget (20 epochs for VAE, 80 epochs for DiT), adding PR to an LDM baseline reduces guided gFID on ImageNet from 3.31 to 2.28, surpassing a DINOv3-aligned VA-VAE (2.44) with negligible overhead. We further demonstrate that PR generalizes to pseudo-labels derived from clustering, continuous text-embedding conditions, and video latents. Together, our findings highlight class geometry as a critical factor in guided generation and take a first step toward CFG-compatible representation learning. Our project page is available at: https://maps-research.github.io/cfg-geometry/.

ml-method.title: Acquisition Function-Guided Generation for Bayesian Optimization over Discrete Spaces
ml-method.subject: cs.LG
ml-method.reason: diffusion bridge enables acquisition-guided sampling for discrete Bayesian optimization
ml-method.abstract: Bayesian optimization (BO) over discrete spaces is challenging due to missing gradients and the sparsity of valid solutions. Latent-space BO sidesteps both issues by fitting a surrogate in the latent space of a generative model, which however substantially complicates the direct incorporation of domain knowledge that is naturally expressed in the original discrete space. In this work, we instead combine a pretrained generative model with a surrogate defined directly in data space, where inductive biases such as domain-specific kernels can be readily incorporated. Rather than maximizing the acquisition function over the discrete design space, our method samples candidates from the generative model under a distribution tilted by the acquisition function. To recover useful gradients for sampling, we embed this tilted distribution into a diffusion bridge that yields a smooth, posterior-averaged acquisition function. This leads to \emph{acquisition function guided generation} (AFGG), which we instantiate with a categorical diffusion model and an autoregressive normalizing flow. Across a broad suite of molecular benchmarks, the diffusion model variant performs on par with leading BO methods, while the flow model variant outperforms state-of-the-art methods in most cases and remains highly competitive otherwise. Our implementation is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/afgg.

ml-method.title: Learning without relearning physical symmetry: an SO(3)-equivariant convolutional network (CNN) on the sphere
ml-method.subject: stat.ML
ml-method.reason: SO(3)-equivariant spherical CNN via steerable filters, exact symmetry
ml-method.abstract: Many of the most important datasets in the physical sciences live natively on the sphere, and these data often carry no preferred position or orientation. Using methods that do not reflect this symmetry leads to far higher simulation requirements, which can be catastrophic for scientific analyses (forcing reliance on cheap, imperfect models that bias results). We present a novel spherical implementation of a gauge equivariant mesh architecture that is specifically designed for the Hierarchical Equal Area isoLatitude Pixelization (\healpix{}) of the sphere. The $\mathrm{SO}(3)$-equivariant convolution is built from steerable filters, parallel transport and spin-weighted features. The architecture supplies the exact symmetry, so the network does not spend training data learning it. The convolution operations are constructed to give provably exact equivariance, given a band-limit. Our full CNNs can achieve SO(3)-invariance error at per-cent-level and lower, which is controlled through well-understood hyperparameters. On benchmarks, our technique gives the most accurate dense gradient regression and competitive cosmic microwave background foreground removal and denoising. The improved simulation efficiency matters most in simulation-based inference (SBI), where high-fidelity simulations are expensive and neural compressors require large training sets, so a fixed budget forces analyses with less accurate simulators. In cosmology lensing SBI, our technique yields the tightest posteriors at matched simulation count. This approach is a novel method that will enable new convolutional neural network analyses, including generative and inference tasks, for processes and data on the sphere.

ml-method.title: Large Diffusion Models Need More Than EMA
ml-method.subject: cs.LG
ml-method.reason: Schedule-Free optimization outperforms EMA for training large diffusion models
ml-method.abstract: Large-scale diffusion models are commonly trained with a constant learning rate (LR) and exponential moving average (EMA), despite the strong performance of LR decay and Schedule-Free optimization in training large language models. We study whether EMA is uniquely suited to diffusion training, or whether stronger alternatives have been underexplored. Our theory shows that averaging a constant-step trajectory has an inherent optimization limitation, whereas LR decay and Schedule-Free optimization admit vanishing stationarity guarantees under standard nonconvex assumptions. Empirically, LR decay and EMA provide complementary benefits: combining decay with EMA further improves the standard baseline at most tested starting points, although the gain remains sensitive to when decay begins. Schedule-Free avoids this timing requirement and consistently outperforms EMA with a constant LR across training stages, achieving both lower fixed-evaluation objectives and better generation quality. Our analysis further shows that all three strategies substantially reduce parameter variability, yet stronger stabilization is not always better: EMA with a constant LR retains comparatively higher parameter variability, while aggressive decay combined with EMA achieves the lowest checkpoint variability but also weakens continued optimization. Schedule-Free substantially reduces parameter variability while preserving more late-stage progress, providing a better balance between parameter stability and continued optimization. Finally, the benefits of Schedule-Free extend beyond pretraining to ReFL and generator-side DMD, demonstrating its transferability across distinct diffusion optimization settings. Overall, our results suggest that large diffusion models need more than parameter averaging alone: effective optimization requires balancing variance reduction with continued optimization.

ml-method.title: DeepD enables efficient genome modeling and controllable long-context sequence generation across domains of life
ml-method.subject: bioinformatics
ml-method.reason: phylogeny-informed MoE genome model generates validated promoters at 1M-token context
ml-method.abstract: Genome foundation models hold great potential for advancing biological research, but modeling diverse complex genomes and generating controllable genome-scale sequences remain challenging. We present DeepD, a phylogeny-informed sparse mixture-of-experts model operating at single-nucleotide resolution over a 1-million-token context while reducing active computation. Pretrained on unselected whole-genome sequences across all domains of life, DeepD learns genic and intergenic sequence features and supports broad sequence-to-function prediction across species. DeepD performs well in human protein fitness and disease variants effect prediction, such as BRCA1 and BRCA2, with particular strength in regulatory regions, such as promoter and transcription-factor binding sites. Expert routing captures exon-intron boundaries, transposable elements, and distal cis-regulatory elements. DeepD also generates experimentally validated core promoters with specified transcriptional strengths. Finally, the Context-Anchor-Body strategy enables generation of complete yeast chromosome sequences and megabase-scale Arabidopsis segments, preserving gene structure and order while introducing variations within natural ranges. Together, DeepD is an efficient genome foundation model that unifies accurate sequence-to-function prediction with controllable genome-scale generation, advancing predictive and generative design of complex genomes.

ml-method.title: CAPO: Compute-Aware Automated Protein-Model Optimization
ml-method.subject: bioinformatics
ml-method.reason: agentic gate-before-you-train system measures fine-tuning feasibility pre-compute
ml-method.abstract: Protein models such as Evolutionary Scale Modeling (ESM), AlphaFold and Boltz have transformed computational protein science, yet a pretrained model rarely transfers to a particular laboratory's assay without adaptation to its data and experimental setting, and that adaptation is technically demanding and spends real compute budget. Existing agentic systems can automate model training, yet typically treat fine-tuning as a reliable tool call: feasibility and cost are estimated rather than measured, and infeasibility is discovered only after compute has been spent. We formulate protein-model adaptation as a gated decision problem: given a task, raw data and a compute budget c_max, a system should decide whether and how to adapt a model before committing expensive computation. We introduce CAPO (Compute-Aware Automated Protein-Model Optimization), a multi-agent system built around one rule: gate before you train. CAPO measures feasibility on the target accelerator, projects cost against the available budget, runs a canary inside the actual training loop and maintains an auditable artifact trail; critically, it can decline an unaffordable adaptation and select a cheaper alternative. We evaluate CAPO, without system changes, on three protein-modeling tasks: (i) SARS-CoV-2 host-range prediction, (ii) hit-to-lead affinity ranking and (iii) temporal variant-effect reclassification. On host range, CAPO partially fine-tuned an 8-million-parameter ESM-2 model to a species-averaged MCC of 0.826, compared with 0.743 for a hand-designed expert transformer; it matched a general coding agent while using 57.4% less GPU time and reduced failed training trials from four to zero. For hit-to-lead affinity ranking, CAPO rejected Boltz-2 fine-tuning and instead trained an assay-calibrated lightweight head over frozen representations, improving ranking on 11 of 15 held-out targets in 1.68 GPU-hours. On temporally held-out ClinVar variants, rank-4 low-rank adaptation of ESM-2 reached an MCC of 0.478, compared with 0.252 for a one-hot baseline and 0.000 for the frozen zero-shot score. These results come from single runs, without a gate ablation and with one generalist-agent comparison. Within those limits, they show that measured admission control can make protein-model adaptation not only automated but selective: deciding what to compute, what not to compute and why.

ml-method.title: LED: Improving Masked Diffusion Language Models by Lookahead Editing
ml-method.subject: cs.LG
ml-method.reason: lookahead editing adds revision capacity to masked diffusion language models
ml-method.abstract: Diffusion large language models (dLLMs) have emerged as a promising alternative to autoregressive language models, enabling non-autoregressive text generation through parallel decoding. Existing dLLMs can be broadly categorized into two families: masked diffusion models (MDMs) and uniform diffusion models (UDMs) In this work, we theoretically show that MDMs are easier to optimize due to their mask-based transition schedule but have lower computational expressivity, whereas UDMs enable iterative state revision and greater expressivity but are substantially harder to train. This trade-off raises a natural question: can we obtain the expressivity of iterative revision without giving up the simple, easy-to-optimize transition schedule of MDMs? Motivated by this analysis, we propose Lookahead Editing (\ours{}), which augments masked diffusion decoding with a rewritable proposal state. At each decoding step, the model performs several lookahead updates to iteratively refine future predictions in this proposal state before committing tokens to the masked sequence. This design introduces a rewritable proposal that uses additional compute to improve expressivity while keeping the simple mask-based transition schedule of MDMs. We fine-tune Qwen2.5-7B and Qwen3-8B to obtain LED-\texttt{7B} and LED-\texttt{8B}, respectively. Across eight benchmarks, LED SFT yields average gains of $+11.4$ and $+7.7$ points over standard MDM SFT. Moreover, using SFT alone, LED-\texttt{8B} outperforms LLaDA2.1-16B Q-mode, which is trained with continued pre-training, supervised fine-tuning, and reinforcement learning.

struct-pred.title: Tryptoline stereoprobe elaboration identifies inhibitors of the GRPEL1-HSPA9 complex.
struct-pred.subject: Nature chemical biology
struct-pred.reason: stereoprobes expose Boltz-2 orthostery-burnout failure at nonorthosteric sites
struct-pred.abstract: Activity-based protein profiling has identified hundreds of human proteins from diverse classes that react at cysteine residues with stereochemically defined electrophilic compounds (stereoprobes). The structure-activity relationships underlying these stereoprobe-protein interactions, however, remain poorly understood. Here, we show that the protein interaction landscape of tryptoline acrylamide stereoprobes can be profoundly altered by structural modifications distal to the acrylamide reactive group. Most stereoprobe liganding events occurred at nonorthosteric sites and evaded assignment by the machine learning-based cofolding model Boltz-2, which instead tended to misplace stereoprobes in orthosteric pockets (an outcome we term 'orthostery burnout'). We found that stereoprobes reacting with C124 in the nucleotide exchange factor GRPEL1 disrupt interactions with the mitochondrial HSP70 chaperone HSPA9/mortalin, leading to impairments in mitochondrial protein import and mitophagy induction. Our results highlight tryptoline acrylamides as a versatile source of covalent ligands targeting nonorthosteric sites on proteins, including tool compounds that perturb the mitochondrial HSP70 chaperone system.

struct-pred.title: Distance-AF Multimer: A Multi-Step Approach for Protein Complex Structure Modeling with User-Defined Distance Constraints
struct-pred.subject: bioinformatics
struct-pred.reason: distance-constrained refinement extends Distance-AF to multimer docking
struct-pred.abstract: The three-dimensional structure of proteins provides essential insight into the molecular mechanisms underlying their function. Many biological activities are mediated through protein interactions, making accurate structural determination of protein complexes important. Despite significant advances in computational protein structure prediction, there are still many cases where protein complexes are not correctly assembled. In particular, there are cases where experimental data, such as distances between residue pairs in interacting proteins are available, yet existing prediction methods fail to produce models consistent with these data. Here, we present Distance-AF Multimer, a method that guides and refines AlphaFold-Multimer docking predictions using user-provided residue pair distance information. This approach extends our previously successful data-guided single-protein modeling method, Distance-AF. Distance-AF Multimer operates in a two-step process, starting from multiple initial conformations and iteratively refining them to satisfy the provided distance constraints. We evaluated Distance-AF Multimer on protein-complex benchmarks spanning different chain counts and docking errors, demonstrating competitive or superior performance compared to other existing deep-learning-based structure prediction methods. In addition to dimer cases, we also demonstrated the potential of Distance-AF Multimer for large-scale protein assemblies containing multiple chains, including those with more than 5 chains.

struct-pred.title: RGI-Toolkit: Differentiable Restraints for Controllable Biomolecular Structure Prediction
struct-pred.subject: bioinformatics
struct-pred.reason: backend-agnostic toolkit for differentiable restraint-guided diffusion inference
struct-pred.abstract: Diffusion-based models have substantially advanced biomolecular structure prediction. Within this framework, restraint-guided inference (RGI) corrects the denoiser output at each reverse-diffusion step using a differentiable restraint loss, allowing available experimental information, stereochemical requirements, or a specified target conformational state to be incorporated into predictions without retraining the model. Here, we present RGI-Toolkit, a general-purpose Python library that makes RGI available for a range of structure predictors. The toolkit consolidates restraint definition, atom selection, loss evaluation, and coordinate optimization into a shared, backend-agnostic engine, limiting predictor-specific code to a thin preprocessing adapter and a single hook in the denoising loop. Restraints on distances, angles, and dihedrals, on deviations from reference structures, and on user-defined reaction coordinates, together with ligand conformer restraints, are all specified in a common configuration format. The toolkit currently supports six predictors, including AlphaFold3. Across all six predictors, conformer restraints eliminated chirality and cis/trans errors in the predicted ligands and improved their local geometry, while geometric and custom restraints systematically shifted the sampled protein conformations toward the specified target states. RGI-Toolkit thus provides a unified framework for integrating experimental information and prior geometric knowledge into structure prediction and for generating biomolecular structures with specified conformational and stereochemical properties.

struct-pred.title: Tensorizing Pairwise Structural Analysis: GPU-Accelerated RMSD and FCC Clustering in HADDOCK3 Without Structural Regression.
struct-pred.subject: bioinformatics
struct-pred.reason: GPU tensor SVD/matmul give 6x speedup for HADDOCK3 RMSD/FCC clustering
struct-pred.abstract: Integrative macromolecular docking pipelines generate thousands of candidate structural decoys, relying on downstream pairwise ensemble analysis, including Root-Mean-Square Deviation (RMSD) matrices and Fraction of Common Contacts (FCC) clustering, to identify biologically relevant binding poses. However, pairwise structural comparisons scale quadratically (O(N^2)), and canonical workflows in HADDOCK3 historically rely on disk-bound trajectory serialization and iterative CPU set operations, creating a quadratic computational and storage bottleneck for large ensembles. Here, we demonstrate that these operations can be reformulated as continuous linear algebra on GPU-resident tensors: structural superposition via batched Singular Value Decomposition (SVD) and residue contact overlap via binary matrix multiplication (M = A A^T). Across empirical benchmarks spanning N = 200 to 10,000 models (evaluating up to 49,995,000 decoy pairs), our GPU implementation achieves a 6.41-fold compute speedup on Apple Silicon (MPS) and up to 12.2-fold end-to-end acceleration in an N = 5,000 ablation on NVIDIA CUDA by eliminating trajectory disk I/O. Crucially, the implementation achieves zero downstream structural regression relative to canonical baselines, preserving identical cluster assignments (Adjusted Rand Index ARI = 1.0000, zero differing assignments) with sub-microangstrom RMSD concordance (Delta_max <= 4.07 x 10^-7 Angstrom on single-precision MPS; machine-precision Delta_max <= 8.88 x 10^-16 Angstrom on double-precision CUDA). The accelerated code, test suites, and benchmarking workflows are openly accessible on GitHub under the Apache-2.0 license.

struct-pred.title: RNAcomp2D: a web tool to execute multiple methods and visually compare predictions of RNA secondary structure
struct-pred.subject: bioinformatics
struct-pred.reason: web tool aggregates and visually compares RNA secondary-structure predictors
struct-pred.abstract: Ribonucleic acids (RNAs) are involved in many important biological processes. In particular, non-coding RNAs are crucial regulators of cellular processes, playing a significant role in gene expression. RNA secondary structure is key to infer their specific function and for understanding how they interact with other molecules. Many computational models have been developed in the last decade to predict the secondary structure, achieving increasingly higher success rates. However, each new method has its own input-output interface, programming language, computational requirements and, sometimes, a dedicated server to run the model or just a source code in a repository. Thus, nowadays it is very hard to obtain predictions from multiple methods and compare them at once. A unified interface is urgently needed, which allows accessing several methods at the same time, visualizing and comparing predictions among them, and also with a reference structure when available. We introduce here RNAcomp2D, a web-based tool that allows users to enter an RNA sequence, or select one from RNAcentral, and obtain predictions of RNA secondary structures using several state-of-theart methods. Both classical thermodynamic methods and the latest deep learning models are packaged in containers and accessible in an unified website. All the predictions, and the reference structure if available, are shown at the same time in a single graphical interface. Moreover, as new models continue to be developed, this tool is designed to be scalable, allowing the addition of more prediction methods in the future. Web server is available at https://sinc.unl.edu.ar/web-demo/rnacomp2d/. Data and source code are available at https://github.com/sinclab/RNAcomp2D

struct-pred.title: HighFold-Lasso: Topology-Guided Prediction of Lasso Peptide Structures Using AlphaFold3
struct-pred.subject: bioinformatics
struct-pred.reason: topology-guided AF3 adaptation for lasso peptide threaded structures
struct-pred.abstract: Lasso peptides are a class of ribosomally synthesized and post-translationally modified peptides (RiPPs) characterized by a mechanically interlocked topology, in which the C-terminal tail is threaded through an N-terminal macrolactam ring formed by an isopeptide bond. This unique topology often confers high thermal stability and resistance to proteolytic degradation. However, the isopeptide linkage, threaded topology, and class-specific disulfide connectivity make lasso peptide structures difficult to reconstruct reliably using general-purpose structure prediction models. Here, we developed HighFold-Lasso, which combines custom covalent connectivity with lasso scaffold-guided adaptive low-noise initialization to enable conditional structure generation guided by lasso conformational priors. On a test set of 52 experimentally determined structures, HighFold-Lasso achieved a 100% lasso topology success rate, with a mean RMSD C-alpha of 1.942 Angstrom for the ring-loop region and 2.375 Angstrom for the full peptide. The framework supports modeling of the four classical lasso peptide classes (I-IV) and can represent noncanonical amino acids, providing computational support for structure-function studies and molecular engineering of lasso peptides.

struct-pred.title: Benchmarking Large Language Models for Assay-Aware Drug-Target Binding Affinity Prediction
struct-pred.subject: bioinformatics
struct-pred.reason: assay-context text improves drug-target binding affinity prediction models
struct-pred.abstract: Machine learning models for molecular discovery often train on bioactivity data from heterogeneous assays, yet assay context is rarely explicitly represented. We investigate whether natural-language assay descriptions provide predictive information beyond molecular and protein representations. We develop ACL-DTI (Assay-aware Contrastive Learning-based Drug Target Interaction) and MAMMAL-AsAP, an assay-context extension of MAMMAL-DTI. Across five triplet-disjoint random splits, assay-aware models achieve competitive or improved performance over assay-agnostic baselines. Among the evaluated models, MAMMAL-AsAP achieves the highest (R^2) of 0.7198 +/- 0.0085. Masking experiments show that ACL-DTI is robust to incomplete assay descriptions, exhibiting the smallest reductions in R^2 among the evaluated models when masking the target name, assay technique, or both: 0.0228 +/- 0.0064, 0.0406 +/- 0.0113, and 0.0620 +/- 0.0190, respectively. These results indicate that assay descriptions contain predictive information not fully captured by molecular structures and protein sequences, and reveal architecture-dependent differences in how this information is exploited.

struct-pred.title: Identification and targeting of a novel drug pocket in the tumour angiogenesis regulator RhoJ
struct-pred.subject: biochemistry
struct-pred.reason: MD reveals allosteric RhoJ pocket, virtual screening finds terconazole binder
struct-pred.abstract: The Rho GTPase RhoJ is a key regulator of tumour angiogenesis and has been identified as a target for anti-angiogenic drug design. Its high sequence conservation with the related Rho GTPase Cdc42 complicates selective drug discovery. RhoJ has a unique N-terminal extension (Asn2-Lys19) that is absent in Cdc42 and other Rho GTPases. Here, we use molecular dynamics simulations to identify a novel allosteric pocket formed by the RhoJ N-terminus and show that this pocket contributes to interactions with key downstream signalling partners. Structure-based virtual screening of small molecules targeting this pocket identified the antifungal terconazole as a potential binder. Computational docking revealed that terconazole occupies the N-terminal pocket, sharing critical contacts with the interface between RhoJ and PAK3, a key interacting partner. To validate this, we developed an optimized bioluminescence resonance energy transfer (eBRET2)-based biosensor to monitor the interaction between RhoJ and PAK3 in live cells and saw that terconazole disrupted the RhoJ:PAK3 interaction in a dose-dependent manner. Together, our MD results show that the RhoJ N-terminal extension assumes structure on binding to PAK3 and contributes to that interaction, while our cellular biosensor data support targeting this pocket to modulate the RhoJ:PAK3 interaction. The ability of terconazole to bind to the N-terminal pocket and disrupt PAK3 binding provides proof of concept for the specific targeting of RhoJ in the development of novel anti-angiogenic drugs.

struct-pred.title: Homology-aware cross-validation strategies for generalization assessment in RNA secondary structure prediction
struct-pred.subject: bioinformatics
struct-pred.reason: critiques homology leakage in RNA secondary-structure cross-validation benchmarks
struct-pred.abstract: RNA secondary structure prediction is a fundamental challenge in bioinformatics, essential for understandingthe functional roles of non-coding RNAs. Recently, deep learning models have transformed the field with impressive results, leading to critical discussions regarding the validity of current crossvalidation strategies. On the one hand, traditional random partitioning yields overoptimistic results due to data leakage from uncontrolled homology. On the other hand, removing every training sequence that even slightly resembles the testing set penalizes learning-based methods, requiring generalization to completely out-of-distribution sequences. While removing sequences and retraining a machine-learned model is straightforward, the experimental data used for development and parameter tuning of classical thermodynamic methods cannot be removed, leaving these methods to benefit from knowledge leakage. Here we critically analyze the cross-validation strategies currently used for RNA secondary structure prediction: random splitting, clustering-based splitting, and leaving one RNA family out for testing. We demonstrate that this last strategy can leave structural patterns present only in the test partition, making the learning task impossible. Overall, we find that the apparent superiority of either type of method is an artifact of the splitting strategy. We propose here two homology-aware strategies: human-learned folds, which exclude from testing the structures already captured by decades of human learning, and similarity folds, which measure performance across the full spectrum of test-totrain similarity. Both enable fair comparisons, applying the same rigorous assessment to classical and learning-based methods.

struct-pred.title: Nucleotide State Regulates Asymmetric Substrate-Binding Protein Docking in a Type II ABC Importer
struct-pred.subject: biochemistry
struct-pred.reason: structures and MD reveal nucleotide-dependent docking cycle in ABC importer
struct-pred.abstract: Type II ABC importers rely on substrate-binding proteins (SBP) to capture nutrients and deliver them to membrane-embedded transporters, but how ATP binding and hydrolysis regulate their interactions remains poorly understood. To address these questions, we determined structures of the Type II small-substrate molybdate importer MolBC-A from H. influenzae in distinct nucleotide-bound states, complemented by molecular dynamics (MD) simulations and functional assays. In a nucleotide-free state, the MolA-MolBC interface is remodeled into a more open conformation, whereas ATP and AMP-PNP binding induce asymmetric conformational changes that preserve the MolA Lobe I interface and disrupt contacts with MolA Lobe II, revealing a previously unresolved partially-docked state. In the ADP-bound state, MolA exhibits the greatest conformational heterogeneity with reduced stable engagement that extends across both lobes. Together these findings define a nucleotide-dependent cycle of asymmetric MolA remodeling and reveal distinct contributions of the two SBP lobes in coupling transporter nucleotide state to SBP engagement.

function-design.title: Recent developments of fluorescent proteins and biosensors driven by cross-disciplinary insights.
function-design.subject: Nature methods
function-design.reason: review of recent fluorescent protein and biosensor engineering advances
function-design.abstract: Since the discovery and application of green fluorescent protein for use as an optical tag, fluorescent proteins (FPs) have changed the way we observe biological signals and processes. FP and fluorescent biosensor design has continued to advance, facilitated by new technologies and developments in chemistry, physics, engineering and screening technologies. We summarize some of the recent developments in FP engineering, focusing on insights that have led to improved photostability or longer wavelengths, among other improvements, highlighting mScarlet as a case study. We also discuss the engineering of new fluorescent biosensors, focusing on the ways in which screening, quantitative imaging, spatial resolution and multiplexing have been improved in recent years. Finally, we conclude with a perspective on what the future holds for the next generation of FPs and biosensors.

function-design.title: Distinct activation mechanisms underlie ligand efficacy at a GPCR
function-design.subject: biophysics
function-design.reason: 400,000-variant DMS maps distinct sequence determinants of GPCR potency vs efficacy
function-design.abstract: Ligands that bind to the same G protein-coupled receptor (GPCR) can produce widely different levels of signaling. These differences in efficacy are central to pharmacology, yet how a receptor sequence determines signaling level remains incompletely understood. Here we develop a deep mutational pharmacology approach to measure how each residue in the -opioid receptor (OR) shapes responses to 15 opioids, yielding ~400,000 measurements of variant effects on signaling and expression, including full concentration-response series for three agonists. Mutational effects on potency are strongest near the orthosteric pocket, whereas effects on efficacy extend through the transmembrane core and intracellular face. Ligands share many functional determinants, but sensitivity to mutation differs with efficacy. As efficacy decreases, the residues required for signaling shift from the binding pocket towards the intracellular face; partial agonists therefore depend on residues that are dispensable for full agonists. Mutations can broadly increase receptor responses, allowing antagonists such as naloxone to produce signaling comparable to a full agonist and increasing the efficacy of partial agonist ligands. Combined mutations can also reorder the relative efficacies of ligands, showing that sequence changes reshape pharmacological differences rather than simply increasing or decreasing all responses together. These findings support a model in which ligands of different efficacy activate the receptor through distinct allosteric mechanisms which are determined by residues distributed across the receptor. Mapping these contributions across diverse ligands with deep mutational pharmacology provides a way to understand how one receptor converts molecular recognition into a range of signaling outputs.

function-design.title: Binding of a Macrocyclic Nonapeptide Inhibitor to Histone Deacetylase 6
function-design.subject: biochemistry
function-design.reason: crystal structure of existing macrocyclic HDAC6 inhibitor, not new design
function-design.abstract: Histone deacetylase 6 (HDAC6) plays an essential role in the regulation of post-translational lysine acetylation. Myriad biological processes depend on the precise regulation of lysine acetylation-deacetylation cycles, and their dysregulation is linked to human pathologies such as cancer and neurodegeneration. Broad-specificity HDAC inhibitors are efficacious in treating disease, but the inhibitors currently approved for clinical use often cause deleterious side effects due to inhibition of multiple HDAC isozymes as well as other zinc enzymes. Cyclic peptides comprise novel platforms that, in principle, can be tailored for affinity and selectivity. A key advantage of cyclic peptide design is the ability to incorporate both canonical and noncanonical amino acids. As part of our program focusing on cyclic peptide HDAC inhibitors, we now report the 1.9-[A] resolution crystal structure of HDAC6 CD2 complexed with macrocyclic nonapeptide 1. The structure reveals zinc coordination by a noncanonical thiolate-containing amino acid, plus direct and water-mediated enzyme-inhibitor hydrogen bonds that contribute to nanomolar inhibitory potency. Structural comparisons with previously reported HDAC6 CD2 complexes with tetrapeptide and octapeptide macrocycles reveal similar networks of direct and water-mediated interactions. Given the surge of interest in cyclic peptide inhibitors, fueled in part by advances in computational design approaches, the crystal structure of the HDAC6 CD2-1 complex sets an important foundation for further development of macrocyclic peptide inhibitors.

function-design.title: Multimodal substrate recruitment enables CTLHMKLN1 E3 ligase to target acetylated N-, C-, and internal degrons.
function-design.subject: Nature communications
function-design.reason: cryo-EM shows MKLN1 beta-propeller domains recognize multiple acetylated degrons
function-design.abstract: The GID/CTLH family of E3 ubiquitin ligases employs several substrate receptor subunits that recruit distinct degrons, but the substrate recognition mechanisms of the CTLHMKLN1 assembly have largely remained elusive. Here, we reconstitute CTLHMKLN1-dependent ubiquitylation of three biochemically distinct substrates - MKLN1 itself, ZMYND19, and FAM72A-recruited UNG2, and determine cryo-EM structures of each substrate bound to MKLN1. The structures reveal how MKLN1's discoidin and Kelch β-propeller domains engage substrates through multivalent contacts. MKLN1 recruits itself through discoidin-Kelch interactions between MKLN1 dimers, forming an assembly that competes with other substrates. ZMYND19 and FAM72A each bind to MKLN1 through loops engaging the discoidin trench domain while their C-terminal Arg residues engage the MKLN1 Kelch central channel, identifying MKLN1 as an Arg/C-degron receptor. The acetylated N-terminus of UNG2 is positioned within a Y-shaped tunnel of FAM72A, defining an adaptor-mediated Ac/N-degron recognition mechanism. Thus, our data reveal how combinatorial deployment of MKLN1 discoidin and Kelch domains enable a single receptor subunit to recognize a diverse substrate repertoire, adding to a complex picture of degron recognition across the GID/CTLH family.

function-design.title: Decoding CBM2 binding modes: how similar folds achieve distinct substrate preferences
function-design.subject: biophysics
function-design.reason: MD and NMR show CBM2 fold-sharing modules bind crystalline substrates in opposite orientations
function-design.abstract: Understanding the mechanisms underlying substrate recognition and selectivity is essential for developing new biotechnological applications of carbohydrate-binding modules (CBMs). Many members of CBM family 2 (CBM2) prefer binding to crystalline substrates and show diverse substrate specificities despite sharing similar folds. We show here that CBM2 specificity cannot be rationalized solely based on sequence and fold. Rather, specific binding of CBM2s to crystalline surfaces depends on a balance of topological complementarity, hydrophobic dehydration, and hydrogen-bonding interactions. We compare the binding modes of ScCBM2 and BaCBM2 on cellulose, chitin, and polyethylene terephthalate (PET) with respect to protein and substrate properties. Using MD simulations and NMR, we explore the CBMs' surface topology, hydration, solvent accessibility, and electrostatics. The results indicate that the two CBMs may bind to crystalline substrates in opposite orientations, and that the interplay between hydrophobic and {pi}-stacking interactions along the aromatic triad and hydrogen-bonding interactions on either side determines their orientation. We further show that higher water density at the aromatic triad correlates with higher substrate affinity. Lastly, we probe the interaction dynamics of BaCBM2 with PET nanoparticles and the monomer bis(2-hydroxyethyl) terephthalate (BHET) using NMR relaxation and solvent paramagnetic relaxation enhancement (sPRE) experiments, revealing a mixture of transient, low-population states involved in PET binding. These insights clarify the interplay among factors that drive CBM2 substrate recognition and highlight the importance of evaluating surface hydration and protein dynamics in future CBM2 studies.

function-design.title: Bivalent Inhibitor Development for a Dynamic Epigenetic Tandem Reader Protein Using a Combinatorial Histone Code
function-design.authors_short: McPherson, J. E., …, Pomerantz, W. C. K.
function-design.subject: biochemistry
function-design.reason: crystallography defines cooperative histone-code recognition by BPTF PHD-bromodomain reader
function-design.abstract: Epigenetic readers are a class of proteins that recognize specific chemical modifications on histones to differentially regulate gene expression. Aberrant expression of readers can drive the progression of many diseases and cancers, making this protein class viable therapeutic targets. Understanding the landscape of histone modifications recognized by reader domains, and the structural mechanisms that drive these molecular recognition events, is crucial for guiding the design of pharmaceutically relevant chemical probes. BPTF contains a plant homeodomain (PHD) finger and tandem bromodomain (BRD). Here, we expand upon previous studies that found the BPTF BRD can engage acetyllysine modifications on the N-terminus of histone H3. We uncover H3K4me3K14ac as the specific modifications recognized by the PHD BRD cassette, which is confirmed by crystallography. Using orthogonal methods, our work explores how these modifications can be read cooperatively, including in cis. We report the first experimental evidence proposing a ligand-induced conformational change between the two reader domains of BPTF, supporting previous computational approaches that have predicted a macromolecular rearrangement. We leverage these structural insights to rationally design a peptide-small molecule conjugate MJ-1 that inhibits both domains of BPTF and overcomes ligandability challenges associated with PHD-finger-containing proteins. The results presented here elucidate the molecular basis of the bivalent recognition of multiply modified histone H3 by BPTF and provide structural insight for developing compounds targeting the PHD finger of BPTF for therapeutic applications.

function-design.title: Chemogenetic ubiquitin E1 inhibitor TAK-243 CRISPR screen uncovers HAPSTR1/HUWE1 axis in chromatin proteostasis and cell cycle control.
function-design.subject: Science advances
function-design.reason: CRISPR screen and structural modeling define HAPSTR1-HUWE1 chromatin proteostasis axis
function-design.abstract: In this study, we sought to comprehensively map ubiquitin signaling networks at the crossroads of cellular proliferation and proteostasis, both crucial in cancer. Genome-wide CRISPR knockout screening in the presence of the ubiquitin E1 inhibitor TAK-243 identified 239 genes whose ablation sensitizes cells to ubiquitination blockade. Follow-up studies reveal a role for the nuclear protein, C16orf72/HECT, UBA, and WWE domain containing E3 ubiquitin protein ligase 1 (HUWE1)-Associated Protein modifying Stress Responses (HAPSTR1), in chromatin proteostasis and DNA replication. We show that HAPSTR1 recruits the E3 ligase HUWE1 to the chromatin, keeping the chromatin-associated proteome in check, and is itself turned over by HUWE1 during cell cycle progression. Structural modeling of the HAPSTR1/HUWE1 complex, supported by mutational analysis, demonstrates that loss of HUWE1 binding renders HAPSTR1 unable to support cellular proliferation when ubiquitin signaling is suppressed. Consequently, HAPSTR1 ablation impairs clearance of chromatin-associated proteins, triggering global transcriptional and proteostatic adaptations. Under diminished ubiquitin signaling, these adaptive mechanisms give way to replication stress and premature S phase entry, culminating in cell cycle collapse and DNA damage. Our findings uncover protein networks exhibiting synthetic lethality with ubiquitin signaling blockade and highlight vulnerabilities of actively proliferating cells to proteostatic imbalance at the chromatin.

function-design.title: ELiAH2: update of the atlas of E3 ligases in human tissues by integrating tissue-specificity and docking properties of ligands for targeted protein degradation
function-design.subject: bioinformatics
function-design.reason: ELiAH2 database prioritizes E3 ligases for targeted protein degradation
function-design.abstract: Targeted protein degradation (TPD), including proteolysis-targeting chimeras (PROTACs), requires coordinated selection of E3 ligases, target proteins, and ligands to achieve efficient and tissue-selective degradation. However, current TPD resources provide limited support for integrating tissue-specific transcriptomic evidence with structural compatibility during early candidate prioritization. Here, we present ELiAH2, an expanded database for transcriptome- and structure-guided prioritization of TPD candidates. ELiAH2 integrates GTEx RNA-seq profiles across 24 human tissues to characterize tissue-specific expression patterns of E3 ligases and target genes. Compared with the previous version, ELiAH, current update presented over 200% of expansion for the number of covered tissues and samples. Previously, E3 ligase-target gene associations were inferred using mutual information-based network analysis, enabling users to explore transcriptomic relationships. To further support structural evaluation, ELiAH2 provides large-scale docking datasets comprising 827,385 E3 ligase-target protein pairs and 7,800,521 protein-ligand docking models, including E3 ligase-ligand and target protein-ligand interactions. Docking scores, ranked interaction tables, gene and ligand identifiers, and downloadable PDB structures are incorporated into the web interface. By combining tissue specificity, E3-target association, protein-protein docking, and protein-ligand docking, ELiAH2 provides a comprehensive resource for narrowing the TPD search space and supporting rational degrader design. ELiAH2 is freely available at https://eliahdb.org.

function-design.title: Capturing domain-level detail of molecular interactions in the IMEx Consortium binding domain data set
function-design.subject: bioinformatics
function-design.reason: IMEx releases large curated dataset of protein binding-domain interaction regions
function-design.abstract: The machinery of the cell depends on physical interactions, between proteins themselves, and between proteins and other biomolecules. The detailed characterisation of these interactions, including the identification of the precise sequence regions mediating binding events, is essential to understand both normal cell biology and disease mechanisms. Protein binding domains are specific regions of a protein sequence that mediate direct contact with a partner and represent a critical layer of functional annotation, bridging sequence, structure, and cellular function. Here we present the IMEx binding domain dataset, a large-scale, manually curated open-access set of molecular interactions assembled over more than two decades by the International Molecular Exchange (IMEx) Consortium. The dataset compiles experimentally derived binding region annotations from peer-reviewed literature, systematically linked to protein-protein interaction (PPI) records and mapped to standardised protein sequences in UniProtKB. We describe the curation model, data format, and content of the dataset, provide a descriptive and comparative analysis, and demonstrate the utility of the dataset as a gold standard for benchmarking interface prediction and variant effect annotation methods. Its integration with genomic variations further offers a route to elucidate the mechanistic basis of disease-associated mutations. The datasets are freely available through IntAct in the dedicated PSI-MI FeatureTAB format at https://ftp.ebi.ac.uk/pub/databases/intact/current/psimitab/features/ and are updated and enhanced with every release.

function-design.title: Determinants of cysteine coverage by chemoproteomics
function-design.authors_short: Riziotis, I. G., …, Bush, J. T.
function-design.subject: bioinformatics
function-design.reason: explainable ML identifies features governing cysteine detectability in chemoproteomics
function-design.abstract: Covalent chemoproteomics has become a powerful route to expanding the druggable proteome, enabling proteome-wide screening of compounds that covalently modify nucleophilic residues, most commonly cysteine. Yet typical experiments detect only 5-18% of the ~250,000 cysteines encoded by the human proteome, and the determinants of this limited coverage remain poorlydefined. Here we combine cysteine featurisation, explainable machine learning (ML) and robust statistical filtering to establish what governs cysteine detectability in iodoacetamide- desthiobiotin (IA-DTB) chemoproteomics. Using a scalable feature-generation pipeline, we computed physicochemical and structural properties for cysteines and the corresponding tryptic peptides and trained models that predict detectability with high accuracy. Shapley analysis identifies protein abundance and intrinsic peptide properties governing LC-MS behaviour as the dominant determinants, whereas cysteine structural descriptors contribute comparatively little, indicating that detection is constrained downstream of probe reactivity. We further introduce a distance-based statistical filter that improves reproducibility across replicates, and show that cell line selection, subcellular fractionation and alternative electrophiles together expand coverage by >30%. More broadly, this work moves optimisation of chemoproteomics workflows from empirical trial-and-error towards rational, data-driven design.

enzyme.title: Scalable Enzyme Reaction Retrieval Enables Metagenomic Biocatalyst Discovery
enzyme.subject: bioinformatics
enzyme.reason: EzHit retrieves enzyme-reaction matches with Mahalanobis geometric confidence scoring
enzyme.abstract: Enzyme catalyzed reactions drive metabolism and enable diverse applications in biotechnology and sustainable synthesis, but assigning catalytic functions to uncharacterized enzymes and finding enzymes for target reactions remain major challenges. Despite recent advances in machine learning, translating enzyme function prediction into systematic discovery across the vast space of uncharacterized proteins and biochemical reactions remains challenging. Here we present EzHit, a lightweight framework for bidirectional enzyme reaction retrieval. Across enzyme annotation, orphan-reaction retrieval and family-specific fine-tuning benchmarks, EzHit achieved strong top-ranked performance and outperformed representative enzyme reaction matching baselines. We further show that Mahalanobis distance based geometric confidence provides more useful reliability estimates than probability-derived uncertainty metrics or evidential learning, enabling confidence-aware prioritization of high scoring candidates. Owing to its efficiency, EzHit was applied to a nearly trillion-scale OMG_Prot50 with RHEA screen, yielding 8.20 billion retained enzyme reaction associations across 30.27 million predicted enzyme sequences. Experimental validation further confirmed the activity of EzHit prioritized metagenomic enzyme candidates for a sparsely annotated reaction. Together, these results establish EzHit as a scalable framework for enzyme annotation, reaction-guided mining and biocatalyst discovery

enzyme.title: Mechanism-guided Discovery of Fluoroacetate Dehalogenase (FAcD) Variants for Enzymatic PFAS Defluorination
enzyme.subject: bioinformatics
enzyme.reason: Boltz-2 co-folding screen ranks dehalogenase variants for PFAS defluorination
enzyme.abstract: Per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) are persistent anthropogenic "forever chemicals" whose strong C-F bonds (~460-533 kJ mol-1) resist defluorination, and the recast EU Drinking Water Directive sets parametric values of 0.10 ug L-1 for the sum of 20 specified PFAS and 0.50 ug L-1 for total PFAS. Here, we present DeFluorX, a mechanism-first pipeline that uses Boltz-2 to co-fold 2,150 bacterial fluoroacetate dehalogenase (FAcD) variants with 26 PFAS and fluoroacetate, generating uniformly high model confidence (rho = +0.08) but poorly tracked catalytic competence. Thus, the complexes were ranked and tiered by SN2-defluorination geometry based on the known mechanism of control of FAcDs RPA1163 with fluoroacetate: Odelta...C-alpha distance and Odelta-C-alpha-F angle; relay; carboxylate clamp; F-stabiliser; F-cradle; and penalties for scissile bond strength, backside occlusion, beta-fluorination and bond multiplicity. The tiering identified eight complexes (med angle 173.2 degrees, distance 2.91 A) with a high probability of degradation, including Alphaproteobacterial enzymes, with mono-, di- and trifluoroacetate attacking at 172-178 degrees versus 163 degrees for the control. We performed WaterMap, restrained 1 us Desmond MD, MM-GBSA and scans of the three WaterMap-aware best MD frames per complex using B3LYP/6-31G** QM/MM. All 12 frames exhibited product-end C-F cleavage with barriers ranging from 1.1 to 11.8 kcal mol-1, and the departing fluoride carried -0.43 to -0.63 e. The Laboratory validation is ongoing.

enzyme.title: Multicatalytic cooperativity enables divergent photobiocatalytic C-C couplings for scaffold diversification
enzyme.subject: biochemistry
enzyme.reason: enzyme-photocatalyst pairing reveals new-to-nature C-C coupling reactivity
enzyme.abstract: Most new-to-nature enzymatic reactions have arisen from mechanism-guided design, whereas synthetically useful, yet unanticipated enzymatic reactivity remains difficult to identify. Here we show that systematic interrogation of enzyme-photocatalyst pairings can reveal emergent reactivity inaccessible to either catalyst alone.
